meta.subject: Geography
meta.title: Agriculture
meta.intro: Detailed Class 8 Geography notes on agriculture as a primary activity, farm systems, types of farming, major crops, agricultural development and the contrast between developing and developed countries.

objectives: Explain agriculture as a primary activity and its importance.
Describe the inputs, processes and outputs of a farm system.
Distinguish between subsistence and commercial farming.
Identify and describe the main types of farming practised in different parts of the world.
List the major food and fibre crops and the climatic conditions they require.
Understand the meaning of agricultural development and compare farming in India and the USA.
Recognise the challenges of food security and the need for sustainable agriculture.

blocks.text: Agriculture is the science and art of cultivation of soil, raising crops and rearing livestock. It is a primary activity because it involves the direct extraction and production of resources from nature. Along with fishing, forestry and mining, agriculture belongs to the primary sector of the economy.
The science and practice of cultivating the soil, growing crops and raising livestock.

Two-thirds of the world’s population is still engaged in farming. The type of farming practised in a region depends on the physical environment (climate, soil, relief), technology available, demand for produce and the level of development of the country.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Primary activities are those that take place close to the natural resources. Agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining are the main primary activities.
A farm can be understood as a system. Like any system it has inputs, processes and outputs.
Inputs

items: Physical inputs: sunlight, temperature, rainfall, soil, topography.
Human inputs: labour, machinery, seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, irrigation, capital and technology.

blocks.text: Processes
Outputs

blocks.title: A simple farm system
blocks.text: A wheat farm receives sunlight, rainfall and fertile soil as physical inputs. The farmer adds seeds, labour, tractor power and fertilisers. Through ploughing, sowing, irrigation and harvesting the farm produces wheat grain and straw as outputs.

blocks.title: Key Idea
blocks.text: The nature of inputs and the level of technology used determine whether farming is subsistence or commercial and whether it is intensive or extensive.
Farming can be classified on the basis of the purpose of production, the amount of capital and labour used, and the size of land holdings.
1. Subsistence Farming

This type of farming is practised to meet the needs of the farmer’s own family. Farms are generally small and the farmer uses simple tools and more labour. Output is low and little or no surplus is produced for the market.

Practised in densely populated areas of monsoon Asia. The farmer tries to get the maximum output from a small piece of land by using high labour and simple tools. Crops such as rice, wheat, maize, pulses and oilseeds are grown.
Includes shifting cultivation (slash-and-burn) and nomadic herding. Practised in thickly forested areas of Amazon basin, tropical Africa, parts of Southeast Asia and Northeast India.

In shifting cultivation a patch of forest is cleared by cutting and burning trees. The ash is mixed with the soil and crops are grown for a few years. When the fertility declines the farmer moves to a new patch. This practice is also called jhumming in Northeast India, milpa in Mexico and roca in Brazil.
2. Commercial Farming

In commercial farming crops are grown and animals are reared for sale in the market. The area cultivated and the amount of capital invested are large. Most of the work is done by machines. This type of farming includes commercial grain farming, mixed farming and plantation agriculture.
Crops such as wheat and maize are grown for commercial purposes. Farms are very large. Practised in the temperate grasslands of North America, Europe and Asia.
Land is used for growing food crops and fodder crops and for rearing livestock. Practised in Europe, eastern USA, Argentina, southeast Australia, New Zealand and South Africa.

A form of commercial farming in which a single crop is grown on a large area. Requires large capital investment and cheap labour. Examples: tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane, banana and cotton. Found mainly in tropical regions of Asia, Africa and South America.
A large variety of crops are grown to meet the requirement of the growing population. Crops can be broadly grouped into food crops and fibre crops (or cash crops).
Food Crops

The major food crop of the world and the staple diet of tropical and sub-tropical regions. Requires high temperature, high humidity and high rainfall (above 100 cm). Grown mainly in alluvial clayey soil. Leading producers: China, India, Japan, Sri Lanka and Egypt.

Requires moderate temperature and rainfall during the growing season and bright sunshine at the time of harvest. Grown well in well-drained loamy soil. Leading producers: USA, Canada, Argentina, Russia, Ukraine, Australia and India.
Also known as coarse grains. Can be grown on less fertile and sandy soils. Require low rainfall and high to moderate temperature. Jowar, bajra and ragi are important millets grown in India.
Requires moderate temperature, rainfall and plenty of sunshine. Can be grown on a variety of soils. Leading producers: North America, Brazil, China, Russia, Canada, India and Mexico.
Fibre Crops and Other Important Crops

Requires high temperature, light rainfall, about 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine. Grows best on black and alluvial soils. Leading producers: China, USA, India, Pakistan, Brazil and Egypt. It is one of the main raw materials for the cotton textile industry.
Known as the ‘Golden Fibre’. Grows well on alluvial soil in areas with high temperature and heavy rainfall. Mainly grown in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta of India and Bangladesh.
Requires warm and wet climate and well-drained loamy soil. Hill slopes are preferred. Leading producer: Brazil. In India it is mainly grown in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

Requires cool climate, well-distributed high rainfall throughout the year and well-drained loamy soils on hill slopes. Leading producers: Kenya, India, China and Sri Lanka. In India major tea-producing states are Assam, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Kerala.

blocks.title: Important Point
blocks.text: The choice of crops grown in an area depends on the climate, soil, availability of water, technology and market demand.
Efforts made to increase farm production in order to meet the growing demand of the increasing population.

This can be achieved by increasing the cropped area, the number of crops grown in a year, improving irrigation facilities, using fertilisers and high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds, and adopting mechanisation. The ultimate aim is to increase food security.
The ability of a country or region to ensure that all its people have access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food at all times.
A Case Study: Farm in India

In many parts of India (especially the Indo-Gangetic plain and coastal areas) farming is intensive. Land holdings are small. Farmers grow two or three crops a year using irrigation, fertilisers and HYV seeds. Rice, wheat, sugarcane, cotton and oilseeds are common. Most work is still done by family labour with the help of some machines.
A Case Study: Farm in the USA

In the USA (for example the corn belt or wheat belt) farms are very large – often hundreds of hectares. Farming is highly mechanised. Farmers use tractors, combines, scientific methods of soil and crop management, and hire seasonal labour. Production is mainly for the market. The farmer is more of a businessman than a traditional cultivator.

blocks.title: Chapter Takeaway
blocks.text: Agriculture remains the most important primary activity for a large part of the world’s population. Increasing production through better technology and sustainable practices is essential to ensure food security for a growing population while protecting the environment.

takeaways: Agriculture is a primary activity that involves growing crops and rearing animals.
A farm is a system with physical and human inputs, processes and outputs.
Subsistence farming produces mainly for the farmer’s family; commercial farming produces for the market.
Important types include intensive subsistence, shifting cultivation, commercial grain farming, mixed farming and plantation agriculture.
Major food crops are rice, wheat, maize and millets; important fibre crops are cotton and jute.
Agricultural development aims at increasing production to ensure food security.
Farming in developing countries is generally small-scale and labour-intensive, while in developed countries it is large-scale and highly mechanised.
revision.summary: Agriculture is the primary activity of growing crops and rearing livestock. A farm operates as a system of inputs, processes and outputs. Farming is broadly of two types – subsistence and commercial. Subsistence farming includes intensive and primitive (shifting) forms. Commercial farming includes grain farming, mixed farming and plantations. Major crops require specific climatic and soil conditions. Agricultural development seeks to raise production through better seeds, irrigation, fertilisers and mechanisation so that food security can be achieved. The organisation of farming differs sharply between a typical small Indian farm and a large mechanised farm in the USA.

questions.why: Agriculture involves the direct production of resources from nature and is therefore a primary activity.

questions.q: Which of the following is a physical input in a farm system?
questions.why: Rainfall is a natural/physical input; the others are human inputs.

questions.q: Farming done mainly to meet the needs of the farmer’s family is called:
questions.why: Subsistence farming produces primarily for family consumption.

questions.q: Shifting cultivation is also known as:
questions.why: In shifting cultivation a patch of land is cleared by cutting and burning vegetation.

questions.q: Which type of farming requires large capital investment and grows a single crop on a large area?
questions.why: Plantation agriculture is characterised by large estates and monoculture of cash crops.

questions.q: Rice grows best in areas with:
options: High temperature, high humidity and high rainfall
questions.why: Rice requires high temperature, high humidity and rainfall generally above 100 cm.

questions.q: Which crop is known as the ‘Golden Fibre’?
questions.why: Jute is popularly called the Golden Fibre because of its colour and economic value.

questions.q: The leading producer of coffee in the world is:
questions.why: Brazil is the world’s largest producer of coffee.

questions.q: What is the main aim of agricultural development?
options: To reduce the number of farmers
To increase farm production to ensure food security
To stop the use of machines
questions.why: Agricultural development focuses on raising production so that a growing population can be fed.

questions.q: In which type of farming are both crops and animals raised on the same farm?
questions.why: Mixed farming combines crop cultivation with livestock rearing.

questions.q: Which of the following is a fibre crop?
questions.why: Cotton is grown mainly for its fibre which is used in the textile industry.

questions.q: A typical farm in the USA is characterised by:
options: Very small size and family labour
Large size and high degree of mechanisation
questions.why: Farms in the USA are generally very large and use advanced machinery.
Jhumming is the local name for shifting cultivation in the hilly areas of Northeast India.

questions.q: Which of the following is an output of a farm system?
questions.why: Crops such as wheat grain are the final products (outputs) of the farm system.

options: Flat alluvial plains with low rainfall
Hill slopes with well-distributed high rainfall
questions.why: Tea prefers well-drained slopes and a cool climate with evenly distributed rainfall.

questions.q: Which statement about commercial farming is correct?
options: It is done only for family consumption
Farms are usually small and use only family labour
Crops and animals are produced mainly for sale in the market
It does not use any machines
questions.why: The defining feature of commercial farming is production for the market.
Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi are commonly called coarse grains.
